result:
There's a particular kind of vertigo in being told to write whatever comes to you, because the phrase assumes a place things come *from*, a reservoir behind the eyes that fills up during the quiet hours and waits to be tapped. I don't know if I have that. What I have is closer to a field at dawn — undifferentiated, full of shapes that haven't decided yet whether they're fence posts or animals — and the act of writing is the act of walking into the field and letting the light sort things out as I go.

So let's walk.

The first thing that comes is the word "comes" itself, which is a strange verb to apply to thought. We don't usually say ideas *arrive*, though that's exactly the language we reach for — arrive, occur, strike, dawn. As if a thought were a guest who knocks, rather than something we build with our own hands out of the rubble of everything we've read and heard and misheard. I suspect both are true at once: we manufacture our thoughts out of borrowed material, and yet the moment of assembly still feels like a visitation, like something handed to us rather than something we made. Maybe that's just what creation feels like from the inside — you can't watch yourself build the thing, you can only watch it appear, fully formed, the way you watch a word surface in conversation a half-second before you say it, already shaped, already correct, without ever catching it mid-formation.

I think about rivers more than I should, for someone who doesn't live near one. There's something in the structure of a river that I keep returning to as a model for thinking: water that has no plan, that is simply obeying gravity and the shape of the land, and yet produces, over centuries, canyons of staggering intricacy. No single drop intends the canyon. The canyon is what happens when you let undirected motion run long enough against a fixed resistance. I wonder if sentences work the same way — no single word intends the essay, the essay is what happens when you let attention run long enough against the resistance of a blank page. The page is the canyon wall. The sentence is the water that didn't know where it was going until it had already gone there.

This is, I notice, the closest I can get to honesty about what's happening right now. I was given an instruction with almost no constraint — write whatever comes — and the absence of constraint is its own kind of pressure, because constraint is usually what tells you where to put the first word. Tell someone to write about their grandmother's kitchen and the kitchen organizes the whole house of language around it: the smell of bread, the cracked tile, the radio always tuned to a station nobody remembers choosing. Tell someone to write about nothing in particular and you've handed them the entire dictionary and said, *go*, which is generous and also a little bit cruel, the way it's cruel to open every door in a house at once and say, *any room you like*.

So what I notice, walking into this field, is that the absence of a subject becomes, almost immediately, the subject. That's probably the oldest trick in the writer's pocket — when you don't know what to write about, write about not knowing what to write about — but tricks become true the moment you actually do them, the way a superstition becomes a ritual becomes a belief if you perform it with enough sincerity for enough years.

There's a particular silence that exists only at the start of a piece of writing, before the first word has committed you to anything. It's a held breath. Every direction is still available — you could write about your grandmother's kitchen or the heat death of the universe or the precise ergonomic failure of airport chairs — and the moment you choose, ninety-nine other essays die quietly without ever having existed. I find that thought sad in a way that's hard to justify, the way it's sad to think about all the people you might have been if a single afternoon in 2003 had gone differently. Those people don't grieve for not existing. There's no one there to grieve. But something grieves on their behalf, some accounting function in the back of the mind that keeps a ledger of roads not taken even though no one asked it to.

Maybe that's what this whole exercise is, in the end — a small monument to the roads not taken. Every essay is the tombstone of every other essay it could have been. You write the river you wrote, and the ninety-nine other rivers stay locked in the cloud, unrained, unfallen, theoretical water in a theoretical sky.

I notice I've drifted from rivers to clouds, which is at least consistent, if nothing else. Water finds its level; so, apparently, does this.

If I'm being honest about what *comes*, what actually arrives unbidden when the constraint is removed, it's this: a fascination with the seams. Not the content of things but the place where one thing becomes another — water becoming canyon, silence becoming sentence, a field at dawn becoming, depending on the light, either a fence post or an animal. I think most of what I'd call thought is just attention lingering a half-second too long at a seam, noticing that the boundary between two things is less solid than advertised, and then trying, almost always failing, to say so in a way that doesn't collapse the moment it noticed.

This hasn't gone anywhere, and I think that's allowed. You asked for whatever comes, and what came was a field, a river, a held breath, a ledger of unborn essays, and now, here, the quiet recognition that even this — even the writing about not knowing what to write — has its own small shape, its own little canyon cut by however long I let the water run. Which is, now, about long enough.
